Faster LLM Inference via Sequential Monte Carlo

Yahya Emara    Mauricio Barba da Costa    Chi-Chih Chang    Cameron Freer    Tim Vieira Affiliation: Cornell University  Makora  MIT  ETH Zürich    Ryan Cotterell Affiliation: Cornell University  Makora  MIT  ETH Zürich    Mohamed S. Abdelfattah
Abstract

Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates language model inference by drafting tokens from a cheap proposal model and verifying them against an expensive target model via rejection sampling. Because rejection truncates the draft block at the first error, throughput degrades when draft and target diverge. Rather than rejecting draft tokens outright, we propose to reweight them. To this end, we introduce sequential Monte Carlo speculative decoding (SMC-SD), which replaces token-level rejection with importance-weighted resampling over a population of draft particles. SMC-SD is a principled approximate inference scheme that trades exactness for additional speed, while preserving theoretical bounds on its per-step approximation error. Because LLM inference is memory bandwidth-bound, the arithmetic needed to draft particles and to score them in parallel comes nearly for free—SMC-SD uses idle compute to turn verification into a vectorized, fixed-size operation with no rollback. Empirically, SMC-SD achieves 2.36×2.36\times speed-up over speculative decoding and a 5.2×5.2\times speed-up over autoregressive decoding, while remaining within 3% of the target model’s accuracy on reasoning, instruction-following, and coding benchmarks.

1 Introduction

Autoregressive generation from neural language models is inherently sequential: each token depends on all previous tokens, so generating a single sequence requires as many serial forward passes through the model as there are tokens in the output. This sequential bottleneck is the primary obstacle to faster inference.

Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023, SD;) addresses this bottleneck by amortizing the cost of target-model calls. At its core, SD is a rejection sampler (Chen et al., 2023): a small draft model—chosen to be significantly cheaper to evaluate—proposes KK-tokens, and the larger target model verifies all KK tokens in a single forward pass, accepting a prefix and rejecting the rest. This rejection criterion ensures that the resulting strings are distributed exactly according to the target, while the speed-up factor is stochastic, depending on the alignment of the draft and target models.

This paper takes a fundamentally different approach to accelerating autoregressive generation. Rather than searching for a faster exact sampler, we devise an approximate sampling scheme whose fidelity to the target can be traded off against speed. The key modification is replacing SD’s token-level rejection step with importance-weighted resampling, making the verification step an instance of sequential Monte Carlo (Doucet et al., 2001; Del Moral et al., 2006; Naesseth et al., 2024, SMC;). Our method reverses the guarantee of SD—approximation quality is stochastic and the speed-up factor is deterministic. We call our method sequential Monte Carlo speculative decoding (SMC-SD) and describe it concretely in § 3.

We derive a closed-form expression for the tokens-per-second (TPS) speed-up factor of SMC-SD with the roofline model (Williams et al., 2009) of the GPU in § 3.1. We show that the roofline model gives a simple characterization of the speed-up factor in both the memory bandwidth-bound and compute-bound regimes.

From a theory perspective, because SMC-SD is ultimately based on importance resampling, non-asymptotic bounds on its approximation error can be obtained using known techniques. In the case of SMC-SD, we show that both the L2L_{2} bias and mean squared error decay linearly in the number of particles and the L1L_{1} bias decays in the root of the number of particles with constants governed by the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence between draft and target model (§ 3.2).

From a systems perspective, SMC-SD presents a novel computation pattern that necessitates designing an inference engine around it. In § 3.3, we use several observations at the intersection of hardware and algorithm to guide the design of our high-throughput SMC-SD inference engine. Both the drafting and verifying stages of SMC-SD use a vectorizable execution structure that map naturally onto GPU hardware and enable greater parallelism than standard speculative decoding. For KV cache management, we observe that all KV cache data movement during the resampling step can be replaced with efficient in-place pointer exchanges, and we reduce the size of the cache by leveraging the shared prefix among particles.

Empirically, SMC-SD achieves up to 2.5×2.5\times the throughput of an optimized implementation of speculative decoding on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023), AlpacaEval (Dubois et al., 2025), and DS1000 (Lai et al., 2022) across both Llama (Team, 2024) and Qwen (Yang et al., 2025) model families, while remaining within 3% of the target model’s accuracy. In a multi-GPU setting, SMC-SD achieves a 2.36×2.36\times speed-up over state-of-the-art speculative decoding and 5.2×5.2\times over the autoregressive baseline. Figure 1 summarizes these end-to-end throughput gains.

2 Language Models and Speculative Decoding

2.1 Language Modeling Background

Let 𝒳{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}} be a finite alphabet, a finite, non-empty set. We call elements of 𝒳{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}} tokens. We write 𝒳∗{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}^{*} for the set of all finite strings over 𝒳{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}, including the empty string ε\varepsilon, and denote individual tokens by x{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x} and strings by 𝒙=x1⋯xT∈𝒳∗{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}={\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{1}\cdots{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{T}\in{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}^{*}. We use the shorthand 𝒙<t=def(x1,…,xt−1){\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}_{<t}\mathrel{\overset{\raisebox{-0.75346pt}{{def}}}{=}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{1},\ldots,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{t-1}) to denote the prefix up to but not including position tt. A language model is a probability distribution pp over 𝒳∗{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}^{*}. Given a language model pp over 𝒳∗{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}^{*}, we define the prefix probability of a string 𝒙{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}} as the total probability of all strings that begin with 𝒙{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}} as follows p→​(𝒙)=def∑𝒙′∈𝒳∗p⁡(𝒙​𝒙′){\overrightarrow{p}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}})\mathrel{\overset{\raisebox{-0.75346pt}{{def}}}{=}}\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{\prime}\in{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}^{*}}p({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{\prime}). The ratio of consecutive prefix probabilities recovers a conditional distribution over the next token x∈𝒳∪{eos}{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}\cup\{{\textsc{eos}}\} where eos∉𝒳{\textsc{eos}}\not\in{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}} is a distinguished symbol:

Every language model admits an autoregressive factorization: p⁡(𝒙)=p→​(eos∣𝒙)​∏t=1Tp→​(xt∣𝒙<t)p({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}})={\overrightarrow{p}}({\textsc{eos}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}})\prod_{t=1}^{T}{\overrightarrow{p}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{t}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}_{<t}). We call a language model that is autoregressively factorized an autoregressive language model. Finally, we say that a language model pp is absolutely continuous with respect to a second language model q{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}, written p≪qp\ll{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}, if q⁡(𝒙)=0⟹p⁡(𝒙)=0,∀𝒙{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}})=0\implies p({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}})=0,\forall{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}.

2.2 Speculative Decoding

Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) accelerates autoregressive inference by applying rejection sampling at the token level. We consider a target model pp and a smaller, faster-to-evaluate draft model q{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q} over the same alphabet 𝒳{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}. Given a draft length KK and the draft–target pair (q,p)({\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q},p), each round proceeds in two phases. In the draft phase, the draft model generates a continuation 𝒅{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}} of up to KK tokens autoregressively from q→\overrightarrow{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}. In the verification phase, the target model scores all KK draft tokens in a single forward pass. Each token dj{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}d}_{j} is accepted with probability αj=min⁡(1,p→​(dj∣𝒙​𝒅<j)/q→​(dj∣𝒙​𝒅<j))\alpha_{j}=\min\bigl(1,\,{\overrightarrow{p}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}d}_{j}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}}_{<j})/\overrightarrow{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}d}_{j}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}}_{<j})\bigr). On the first rejection, the token is resampled from the residual distribution and all subsequent draft tokens are discarded; if every token is accepted, a bonus token is drawn from p→(⋅∣𝒙𝒅){\overrightarrow{p}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}}). In either case, every round produces at least one token whose distribution involves the target model. This procedure guarantees that the output is distributed exactly according to pp (Leviathan et al., 2023); the full pseudocode is given in Appendix A. The effective speed-up depends on the acceptance rate: the closer q{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q} is to pp, the more tokens survive per round.

3 Sequential Monte Carlo Speculative Decoding

Sequential Monte Carlo (Doucet et al., 2001; Del Moral et al., 2006; Naesseth et al., 2024, SMC;) runs a population of NN particles {𝒙(n)}n=1N\{{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{N}; each particle is a string that we intend to keep extending. Each particle alternates between three operations at each step tt:

  1. 1.

    Extend: sample xt(n)∼q→(⋅∣𝒙(n)){\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{t}^{(n)}\sim\overrightarrow{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}) for each particle, appending the token to 𝒙(n){\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}.

  2. 2.

    Reweight: update each weight by wt(n)←wt−1(n)⋅p→​(xt(n)∣𝒙<t(n))/q→​(xt(n)∣𝒙<t(n)){\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}_{t}^{(n)}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}_{t-1}^{(n)}\cdot{\overrightarrow{p}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{t}^{(n)}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}_{<t})/\overrightarrow{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{t}^{(n)}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}_{<t}).

  3. 3.

    Resample: if the effective sample size (ESS) falls below a threshold, draw new ancestor indices a1,…,aNa_{1},\ldots,a_{N} independently from a categorical distribution over {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\} with probabilities proportional to the normalized weights w¯(1),…,w¯(N)\overline{{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}}^{(1)},\ldots,\overline{{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}}^{(N)}, set 𝒙(n)←𝒙(an){\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(a_{n})} for all nn, and reset all weights to 1/N1/N.

Resampling concentrates computation on promising prefixes and prevents weight degeneracy from rendering the particle population uninformative. The effective sample size (ESS) (Huggins, 2014) quantifies how many particles contribute meaningfully:

ESS=(∑n=1Nw(n))2∑n=1N(w(n))2.\mathrm{ESS}\;=\;\frac{\bigl(\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}^{(n)}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}\bigl({\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}^{(n)}\bigr)^{2}}. (2)

The ESS satisfies 1≤ESS≤N1\leq\mathrm{ESS}\leq N: when ESS≈N\mathrm{ESS}\approx N, all particles contribute meaningfully; when ESS\mathrm{ESS} collapses toward 11 (weight degeneracy), a single particle dominates. The resample step in SMC is triggered when ESS\mathrm{ESS} falls below a threshold, pruning low-weight particles and duplicating high-weight ones to maintain sample diversity.

The SMC-SD Algorithm.

We instantiate the SMC framework for speculative decoding in Algorithm 1: the target is pp, the proposal is a cheaper draft model q{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}, and one round extends every particle by a draft of up to KK tokens. At the start of each round, the particle population represents a set of partially generated strings 𝒙(1),…,𝒙(N){\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(N)}; particles may share ancestry through earlier resampling steps, but they need not share the same current prefix. For a weighted particle population {(𝒙(n),w(n))}n=1N\{({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)},{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}^{(n)})\}_{n=1}^{N}, draft length KK, and ESS threshold η∈[0,N]\eta\in[0,N], a single round proceeds as in Algorithm 1. Unlike SD, no token-level accept/reject chain truncates a draft midway; every particle is extended by exactly KK tokens per round (Figure 2).

Each particle independently drafts KK sequential tokens from its own current prefix under q{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}, then the target model pp scores all NN sequences in a single batched forward pass and generates a bonus token. The resulting block weights update the particle population, and a low-ESS resampling step duplicates high-weight trajectories while pruning low-weight ones. The round updates the internal particle population block by block; after the final round, one complete sequence is sampled from the terminal normalized weights and returned as the model output. That is, SMC-SD maintains latent particle trajectories during generation and samples the returned sequence only at termination.

3.1 Speed-up Analysis

We analyze SMC-SD TPS under the roofline model (Williams et al., 2009), which classifies a workload according to its arithmetic intensity, or the floating-point operations (FLOPs) used per byte of memory loaded for the workload. Whether a workload is memory bandwidth-bound or compute-bound depends on whether its arithmetic intensity is greater than or less than the ridge point of the hardware, or its peak FLOPs per memory bandwidth. Let BB denote the number of independent user requests served concurrently (the batch size), and let the effective batch size denote B​NBN, the total number of particles across all requests. The target model’s forward pass processes B​N​(K+1)BN(K{+}1) tokens per round: NN particles per request, each extended by KK draft tokens plus one bonus token. Let c=Tq/Tp≪1c=T_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}/T_{p}\ll 1 be the draft-to-target decoding-time ratio; under the roofline model, c≈ρ=def𝒫q/𝒫pc\approx\rho\mathrel{\overset{\raisebox{-0.75346pt}{{def}}}{=}}\mathcal{P}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}/\mathcal{P}_{p} (assuming the draft and target have the same quantization), since memory-bound latency is proportional to parameter count. Let RR denote the effective batch size (in tokens) at which a forward pass reaches the ridge point; this depends only on the hardware and quantization format. Below, we characterize the speed-up factor depending on whether the verification pass is memory-bound or compute-bound (proofs in Lemmas D.3 and D.4).

Memory-bound regime. When B​N​(K+1)≤RBN(K{+}1)\leq R, the target scores all B​N​(K+1)BN(K{+}1) tokens in a single weight-load and the speed-up over autoregressive decoding is

S(mem)=K+1ρ​K+1,S^{(\text{mem})}=\frac{K+1}{\rho K+1}, (3)

independent of B​NBN—particles are “free.”

Compute-bound regime. Once B​N​(K+1)BN(K{+}1) exceeds RR, the target pass becomes compute-bound. Writing ρ^​(B​N)=max⁡(ρ,ρ​B​N/R)\hat{\rho}(BN)=\max(\rho,\rho BN/R) for the effective draft cost ratio, the speed-up falls to

S(comp)=K+1ρ^​(B​N)​K+B​N​(K+1)/R,S^{(\text{comp})}=\frac{K+1}{\hat{\rho}(BN)\,K+BN(K{+}1)/R}, (4)

which degrades linearly in the effective batch size after the ridge point has been reached.

Figure 3 shows the theoretical speed-up for multiple values of NN and KK. The figure uses a Llama-1B→\,\to\,8B pair. The speed-up factor increases with respect to KK up until the ridge point is reached; at which point, the speed-up becomes approximately constant. The speed-up factor is constant with respect to NN in the memory-bandwidth bound regime, but degrades linearly once the workload becomes compute-bound.

3.2 Characterizing SMC-SD Approximation Error

Because SMC-SD is an approximate sampler, it is important to characterize its approximation quality. Fortunately, since SMC-SD is based on importance sampling, bounds on its divergence from a target distribution can be obtained using known techniques (Agapiou et al., 2015; Del Moral et al., 2006). If ff is any evaluation metric bounded in [0,1][0,1], then |𝔼p^N[f]−𝔼p[f]|≤‖p^N−p‖1|\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}}}[f]-\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{p}[f]|\leq\|{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}}-p\|_{1}: controlling the total variation distance between the SMC-SD output p^N{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}} and the target pp directly controls the gap in any bounded downstream metric. We establish bounds on this distance as a function of the number of particles NN. We also bound the effective sample size as a function of the draft length KK in B.2, which informs the choice of operating parameters for a given compute budget.

At each round of Algorithm 1, the weighted particle population defines an empirical distribution over generated sequences. Let p^N{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}} denote this importance resampling distribution:

p^N(𝒙)=def∑n=1Nw(n)∑m=1Nw(m)𝟙{𝒙(n)=𝒙}.{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}})\mathrel{\overset{\raisebox{-0.75346pt}{{def}}}{=}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}^{(n)}}{\sum_{m=1}^{N}{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}^{(m)}}\mathbbm{1}\{{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}={\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\}. (5)

As N→∞N\to\infty, since p^N{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}} and pp are discrete, p^N{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}} converges to pp in total variation distance almost surely (Del Moral et al., 2006). For finite NN, however, p^N{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}} is a random distribution that depends on the particular draw of proposals and resampling decisions.

Let p¯N=def𝔼[p^N]{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\overline{p}_{N}}\mathrel{\overset{\raisebox{-0.75346pt}{{def}}}{=}}\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}}] denote the expected importance resampling distribution, where the expectation is over all randomness in the NN particles. We decompose the error of p^N{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}} into bias and variance. The bias measures systematic error—how far the expected behavior p¯N{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\overline{p}_{N}} deviates from pp:

    BiasL22(p^N)=∥p¯N−p∥22=O((1+χ2(p∥q))/N)\mathrm{Bias}_{L^{2}}^{2}({\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}})=\|{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\overline{p}_{N}}-p\|_{2}^{2}=O\left((1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}))/N\right).

  3. 3.

    MSE(p^N)=𝔼[∥p^N−p∥22]=O((1+χ2(p∥q))/N)\mathrm{MSE}({\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}})=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[\|{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}\widehat{p}_{N}}-p\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]=O\left((1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}))/N\right).

Theorem 3.1 bounds the error of importance resampling (proof and supporting lemmata in Appendix B), the primitive that each round of SMC-SD applies to its particle population. For a single round, both the L2L^{2} bias and mean squared error decay as O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) in the number of particles, and the L1L^{1} bias decays as O⁡(1/N)O(1/\sqrt{N}), with constants governed by the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence between draft and target. These per-round bounds give practitioners a concrete lever—increasing NN tightens the approximation at each step—but they do not directly characterize the error of the full multi-round SMC procedure, where resampling introduces inter-particle correlations and path degeneracy may accumulate across rounds. We leave bounding the error of the resampling step of SMC-SD to future work. We validate empirically in § 4 that the per-round guarantees translate into strong end-to-end accuracy across benchmarks.

3.3 High-Throughput SMC-SD Engine Design

SMC-SD is not merely an algorithm that happens to run on GPUs—its vectorized structure maps onto the batch-parallel execution model of modern accelerators and makes use of modern optimizations on inference engines including dynamic batching, PagedAttention, and RadixAttention (Yu et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024). As such, we build our SMC-SD engine as a fork of SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024). We describe our high-throughput inference engine for SMC-SD, organized around a series of observations at the intersection of algorithm and hardware.

Observation 1: SMC-SD converts under-utilized compute into speed.

Autoregressive decoding is heavily memory bandwidth-bound: each token requires loading the full model weights yet performs only a single vector–matrix multiply. The arithmetic intensity, the FLOPs performed per byte of memory load, for a forward pass of a language model quantized to bb bytes per parameter remains at just AIAR=2/b\mathrm{AI}_{\mathrm{AR}}=2/b. Standard speculative decoding increases the arithmetic intensity by a factor of KK but both methods remain far below the roofline ridge points of modern GPUs—312 for A100, 412 for H200, 584 for B300 in FP16 (NVIDIA Corporation, 2020; NVIDIA Corporation, 2024b; NVIDIA Corporation, 2024c; NVIDIA Corporation, 2024a)—leaving the vast majority of available compute idle.

SMC-SD closes this gap by leveraging parallelism along the batch-wise and sequence-wise axes. The draft model uses dynamic batching to concurrently generate NN tokens at a time in lockstep, followed by the target model scoring a block of N⁡(K+1)N(K{+}1) tokens using a single re-prefill step. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the target model’s parameter count, bb the bytes per parameter (b=2b{=}2 for FP16, b=1b{=}1 for INT8), and ρ=𝒫q/𝒫p\rho=\mathcal{P}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}/\mathcal{P}_{p} the draft-to-target parameter ratio. Over a full SMC-SD cycle, the arithmetic intensity is (proofs in Appendix D)

AIcycle=2​N​(ρ​K+K+1)b⁡(ρ​K+1)≈2​N​(K+1)bwhen ​ρ≪1,\text{AI}_{\text{cycle}}=\frac{2N(\rho K{+}K{+}1)}{b(\rho K+1)}\;\approx\;\frac{2N(K{+}1)}{b}\quad\text{when }\rho\ll 1, (9)

an ≈N×\approx N\times increase over standard SD. For Llama-3.1-70B in FP16 with N=8N{=}8 and K=16K{=}16, AIcycle≈136\text{AI}_{\text{cycle}}\approx 136 compared to just 1717 for standard SD with the same KK.

Observation 2: Pointer operations turn prefix-sharing into compute and memory gains.

The resampling step in SMC-SD introduces a novel challenge in inference engine design. When resampling duplicates a high-weight particle, a naïve implementation would require KV-cache data movement across particles and re-prefill for the duplicated sequences. In SMC-SD, we avoid both of these costs by exploiting the prefix-sharing structure together with page-based KV-cache management (Kwon et al., 2023) and RadixAttention (Zheng et al., 2024). Specifically, duplicated particles share exactly the same prefix as their ancestors up to the resampling point, so the engine can perform resampling by copying page metadata and incrementing the reference counts rather than copying the underlying KV tensors directly. As a result, resampling is implemented as an O⁡(ℓseq)O(\ell_{\text{seq}}) page-metadata operation, rather than an O⁡(ℓseq×dmodel)O(\ell_{\text{seq}}\times d_{\text{model}}) KV-tensor copy. Exploiting prefix sharing not only avoids KV-cache data movement and reduces FLOPs, but also lowers memory usage. Empirically, for the Llama-1B→\,\to\,8B, N=8N{=}8, K=16K{=}16 configuration, our optimization yields a 72.3% reduction in KV-cache usage.

4 Experiments

We characterize the speed–accuracy Pareto frontier of SMC-SD on a single H100 GPU across GSM8K, MATH500, AlpacaEval, and DS1000 (Dubois et al., 2025; Cobbe et al., 2021; Lai et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2023). We test two model families—Llama 3.2-1B→\to3.1-8B, and Qwen 0.5B→\to14B (SD) versus Qwen 3B→\to14B (SMC-SD)11 1 For Qwen, the 0.5B draft makes for a faster speculative decoder than 3B because the smaller draft is faster and SD’s acceptance rates do not justify the larger model. SMC-SD, by contrast, benefits from the stronger 3B proposal, so we compare each method with its best draft model.—to demonstrate that SMC-SD’s gains are consistent across architectures and draft-to-target size ratios.

GSM8K, MATH500, AlpacaEval, and DS1000.

Figure 4 shows the speed–accuracy Pareto frontier for SMC-SD and optimized SD on GSM8K, MATH500, AlpacaEval, and DS1000. Across all four benchmarks and both model families, the SMC-SD frontier lies above and to the right of the SD baseline, indicating simultaneous improvements in throughput and accuracy or favorable tradeoffs between the two. Table 1 quantifies the gains at two operating points: iso-accuracy (the fastest SMC-SD configuration within 3 percentage points of SD’s accuracy) and max speed (within 10 percentage points). At iso-accuracy, SMC-SD achieves 1.11.1–2.5×2.5\times the throughput of SD; allowing a modest accuracy relaxation widens this to up to 3.4×3.4\times (Appendix C).

Despite being an approximate sampler, SMC-SD maintains strong downstream accuracy: every point on the Pareto frontier in Figure 4 remains within 15% of the target model’s accuracy. The throughput gains come from a structural difference in how SMC-SD uses the target forward pass. In standard SD, the first rejected token truncates the draft and triggers a KV-cache rollback, so the number of tokens produced per round is variable and often much less than K+1K{+}1. SMC-SD always produces exactly K+1K{+}1 tokens per particle per round—there is nothing to roll back.

Multi-GPU throughput.

We deploy SMC-SD on a Llama 3.2-1B→\,\to\,Llama 3-70B draft-target pair across 4 H100 GPUs. Figure 1 summarizes the results: SMC-SD achieves 342 tok/s, a 5.2×5.2\times speed-up over the autoregressive baseline and a 2.36×2.36\times speed-up over optimized tree-based speculative decoding (SGLang SD). Figure 5 shows throughput per GPU as a function of batch size for both the 1B→\to8B and 1B→\to70B pairs; SMC-SD leads across most batches tested.

5 Related Work

SMC for Language Models.

Recent work has applied SMC to large language models for constrained generation: steering outputs toward syntactic constraints (Loula et al., 2025; Xefteri et al., 2025), semantic specifications (Lew et al., 2023), or reward-defined posteriors (Zhao et al., 2024). In these settings, the target is a posterior p⁡(x∣constraint)p(x\mid\text{constraint}) and the proposal is the unconstrained language model. SMC-SD repurposes the same machinery for inference acceleration: the target is pp itself and the proposal is a faster draft model q{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}.

Exact speculative decoding.

Tree decoding algorithms (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b) extend standard SD by proposing a tree of tokens at each position, increasing the expected number of accepted tokens while preserving exact sampling. SMC-SD trades exactness for speed via a tunable approximation.

Approximate speculative decoding.

Several methods relax exactness through heuristic acceptance criteria. FSD (Holsman et al., 2025) accepts tokens based on draft–target divergence; FLy (Li et al., 2025a) uses an entropy gate with a deferred acceptance window; Judge Decoding (Bachmann et al., 2025) trains a judge network to replace rejection sampling. All retain a per-token accept/reject gate: a single rejection truncates the block, each token’s contribution is binary, and outputs are variable-length. SMC-SD instead assigns each block a continuous importance weight, produces a fixed number of tokens per round, and provides asymptotic convergence guarantees—all without additional training.

Complementary strategies.

Several orthogonal techniques can be combined with SMC-SD. On the drafting side, EAGLE (Li et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025c) conditions the draft model on target-model embeddings, Medusa (Cai et al., 2024) attaches parallel decoding heads, and DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) uses a diffusion model—all producing higher-quality or faster proposals that would directly benefit SMC-SD. On the scheduling side, Specdec++ (Huang et al., 2025) adaptively modulates speculation length and SSD (Kumar et al., 2026) asynchronously overlaps drafting and verifying; analogous adaptive strategies over NN and KK are a natural extension of SMC-SD. All results use the optimal temperature parameters for each task for both SMC-SD and SD.

6 Conclusion

We presented SMC-SD, an algorithm that accelerates LLM inference by replacing speculative decoding’s token-level rejection with importance-weighted resampling over a population of draft particles. We established non-asymptotic error bounds showing that the bias and MSE of the importance sampling component of SMC-SD decays as O⁡(1/N)O(1/N), and we demonstrated empirically that SMC-SD achieves 2.36×2.36\times the throughput of optimized speculative decoding and 5.2×5.2\times over autoregressive decoding in a multi-GPU setting, while remaining within 3% of the target model’s accuracy across reasoning, instruction-following, and coding benchmarks.

Beyond acceleration, a key property of SMC-SD is that the same importance-weighting machinery can target distributions beyond pp itself. Given a factor Ψ\Psi, SMC-SD can sample approximately from distributions of the form π(x1:T)∝p(x1:T)⋅Ψ(x1:T)\pi(x_{1:T})\propto p(x_{1:T})\cdot\Psi(x_{1:T}), provided one can define a sequence of potential functions {ψt}t=1T\{\psi_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} from which properly weighted pairs (wt,xt)∼ψt({\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}_{t},x_{t})\sim\psi_{t} can be drawn (Del Moral et al., 2006). The usual SMC convergence guarantees carry over. Three natural instantiations are:

  • •

    Power sampling (Ψ=pα−1\Psi=p^{\alpha-1}, targeting π∝pα\pi\propto p^{\alpha}). Unlike per-token temperature scaling, this tempers the distribution over entire sequences. Appendix F shows a 10% Pass@1 improvement on MATH500 with Llama-1B→\,\to\,8B and a dominating Pass@kk for k>1k>1.

  • •

    Constrained generation (Ψ=𝟏[x∈𝒜]\Psi=\mathbf{1}[x\in\mathcal{A}]). Hard constraints—syntactic validity, format compliance, length bounds—can be enforced while preserving the target’s distribution conditioned on the constraint. Prior work (Lew et al., 2023; Loula et al., 2025; Xefteri et al., 2025) has shown that such constraints can improve accuracy on coding benchmarks; incorporating them into SMC-SD could simultaneously increase downstream performance while accelerating inference.

  • •

    Reward-weighted decoding (Ψ=exp⁡(β⋅R⁡(x))\Psi=\exp(\beta\cdot R(x)), targeting π∝p⋅eβ​R\pi\propto p\cdot e^{\beta R}). This targets the KL-regularized optimal policy arising in RLHF without fine-tuning, which is relevant for agentic settings where the same base model must be steered toward different objectives.

Standard speculative decoding cannot express any of these: it requires knowledge of the normalizing constant of the target, which is unavailable for this class of distributions.

On the systems side, much work remains to achieve the theoretical roofline model speedup of SMC-SD demonstrated in Figure 3. First, there are opportunities to overlap resampling with drafting to remove its performance overhead altogether. This can be done by preemptively speculating the result of the ESS threshold, and beginning the next round of drafting accordingly. Furthermore, the draft and target models can be disaggregated across hardware, and asynchronously dispatch drafting and scoring calls. Second, by allowing NN and KK to vary dynamically, SMC-SD can adapt to underlying hardware and workload characteristics, enabling runtime exploration of its tunable Pareto frontier. Finally, SMC-SD reflects a trend in co-designing inference algorithms with asymmetric hardware scaling—compute grows faster than memory bandwidth (Zadouri et al., 2026). For instance, the Blackwell GPU architecture significantly increases FLOPS over the previous generation of Hopper GPU and keeps memory bandwidth approximately equal; this increased compute budget makes it an ideal target for SMC-SD.

Appendix A Speculative Decoding Algorithm

We give the full pseudocode for the standard speculative decoding procedure of Leviathan et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023), referenced in § 2.2. Given a draft length KK and the draft–target pair (q,p)({\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q},p), each iteration proceeds in two phases. In the draft phase, given the string generated so far 𝒙{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}, the draft model generates a draft continuation 𝒅{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}} of at most KK tokens autoregressively from q→\overrightarrow{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}. In the verification phase, the target model scores all draft tokens in a single forward pass. Each draft token dj{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}d}_{j} is then tested sequentially using the standard rejection sampling criterion: it is accepted with probability αj=min⁡(1,p→​(dj∣𝒙​𝒅<j)/q→​(dj∣𝒙​𝒅<j))\alpha_{j}=\min\bigl(1,{\overrightarrow{p}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}d}_{j}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}}_{<j})/\overrightarrow{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}d}_{j}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}}_{<j})\bigr). On the first rejection, the token is resampled from the residual distribution max(0,p→(⋅∣𝒙𝒅<j)−q→(⋅∣𝒙𝒅<j))\max\bigl(0,\;{\overrightarrow{p}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}}_{<j})-\overrightarrow{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}}_{<j})\bigr) and the draft is truncated. If every token passes, a bonus token is drawn from p→(⋅∣𝒙𝒅){\overrightarrow{p}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{d}}).

Appendix B Proofs

B.2 ESS Rate Results

Because the importance weight of a bonus particle depends only on the KK draft tokens (the bonus token cancels between the target and proposal densities), the ESS is governed by the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence between the KK-token block distributions pKp_{K} and qK{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}—not the (K+1)(K\!+\!1)-token distributions.

Theorem B.3 (ESS Rate).

Under the assumption χ2(pK∥qK)<∞\chi^{2}(p_{K}\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K})<\infty, the ESS fraction converges almost surely:

ESSNN→a.s.11+χ2(pK∥qK)\frac{\mathrm{ESS}_{N}}{N}\;\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{a.s.}\;}\;\frac{1}{1+\chi^{2}(p_{K}\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K})} (36)

Crucially, the divergences are between the KK-token block distributions, even though each particle produces K+1K+1 tokens.

Proof of Theorem B.3.

By the strong law of large numbers, 1N​∑i=1Nwi→a.s.𝔼qK[w]=1\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}_{i}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}}[{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}]=1 and 1N∑i=1Nwi2→a.s.𝔼qK[w2]=1+χ2(pK∥qK)\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}_{i}^{2}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}}[{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}^{2}]=1+\chi^{2}(p_{K}\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}). Therefore

ESSNN=(1N​∑iwi)21N​∑iwi2→a.s.(𝔼qK[w])2𝔼qK[w2]=11+χ2(pK∥qK).\frac{\mathrm{ESS}_{N}}{N}=\frac{\bigl(\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}_{i}\bigr)^{2}}{\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}_{i}^{2}}\;\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{a.s.}\;}\;\frac{(\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}}[{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}])^{2}}{\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}}[{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}^{2}]}=\frac{1}{1+\chi^{2}(p_{K}\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K})}. (37)

∎

If (as a simplified model) the KK tokens are independent and identically distributed, the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence factors as an exact power:

Proposition B.4 (I.I.D. Case).

Suppose pK=p⊗Kp_{K}=p^{\otimes K} and qK=q⊗K{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}={\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}^{\otimes K} (i.i.d. tokens)22 2 The exponential decay in Proposition B.4 assumes i.i.d. tokens and is likely loose for autoregressive models, where successive tokens are strongly correlated given the prefix. The exact ESS limit in Theorem B.3 holds without this assumption; understanding how the block χ2\chi^{2}-divergence χ2(pK∥qK)\chi^{2}(p_{K}\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}) grows with KK under realistic autoregressive dependencies is an interesting direction for future work.. Then

1+χ2(pK∥qK)=(1+χ2(p∥q))K.1+\chi^{2}(p_{K}\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K})=\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{K}. (38)

Therefore ESSN/N→(1+χ2(p∥q))−K\mathrm{ESS}_{N}/N\to\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{-K}. Each particle produces K+1K+1 tokens but the ESS penalty is only (1+χ2(p∥q))−K\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{-K}, not (1+χ2(p∥q))−(K+1)\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{-(K+1)}.

Proof of Proposition B.4.

By independence,

𝔼qK[w2]=∑𝒙1:KpK(𝒙1:K)2qK(𝒙1:K)=∏t=1K∑xp​(x)2q⁡(x)=(1+χ2(p∥q))K.∎\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}}[{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}^{2}]=\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}_{1:K}}\frac{p_{K}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}_{1:K})^{2}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}_{K}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}_{1:K})}=\prod_{t=1}^{K}\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}}\frac{p({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x})^{2}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x})}=\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{K}.\qed (39)
Corollary B.5 (Bonus Token Efficiency Gain).

In the i.i.d. setting, without the bonus token, generating K+1K+1 tokens entirely from the draft model would give ESS fraction (1+χ2(p∥q))−(K+1)\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{-(K+1)}. The bonus token improves this by a multiplicative factor of (1+χ2(p∥q))\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr):

(ESS/N)with​bonus(ESS/N)without​bonus=1+χ2(p∥q).\frac{(\mathrm{ESS}/N)_{\mathrm{with\;bonus}}}{(\mathrm{ESS}/N)_{\mathrm{without\;bonus}}}=1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}). (40)
Proof of Corollary B.5.

Without the bonus token, all K+1K+1 tokens are drafted from q{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}, so the ESS fraction converges to (1+χ2(p∥q))−(K+1)\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{-(K+1)} by Proposition B.4 applied with draft length K+1K+1. With the bonus token, the ESS fraction converges to (1+χ2(p∥q))−K\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{-K} by Proposition B.4. The ratio is

(1+χ2(p∥q))−K(1+χ2(p∥q))−(K+1)=1+χ2(p∥q).∎\frac{\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{-K}}{\bigl(1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q})\bigr)^{-(K+1)}}=1+\chi^{2}(p\|{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}).\qed (41)

Appendix D Hardware Utilization and Speedup Proofs

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the target model’s parameter count, bb the bytes per parameter, ρ=𝒫q/𝒫p\rho=\mathcal{P}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}/\mathcal{P}_{p} the draft-to-target parameter ratio, c=Tq/Tp≪1c=T_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}/T_{p}\ll 1 the draft-to-target decoding-time ratio. Let BB denote the number of independent user requests served concurrently (the batch size), and let B​NBN denote the effective batch size—the total number of particles across all requests. In the memory-bound regime c≈ρc\approx\rho. In one SMC-SD step, the draft model runs KK sequential forward passes (one per token position, with all B​NBN particles batched), taking c​Tp​KcT_{p}K seconds. The target model scores all B​N​(K+1)BN(K{+}1) tokens (including bonus tokens) in a single forward pass. The resampling step is negligible.

D.1 Arithmetic Intensity

Lemma D.1 (Target-pass arithmetic intensity).

The arithmetic intensity of the target model’s forward pass in one SMC-SD cycle is

AItarget=2​B​N​(K+1)b​FLOPs/byte.\text{AI}_{\text{target}}=\frac{2BN(K{+}1)}{b}\;\;\text{FLOPs/byte}. (42)
Proof.

Using the standard approximation that a forward pass through a model with 𝒫\mathcal{P} parameters requires 2​𝒫2\mathcal{P} FLOPs (one multiply-add per parameter), the target pass processes B​N​(K+1)BN(K{+}1) tokens in one invocation—B​N​KBNK draft tokens plus B​NBN bonus tokens carried over from the previous round—for a total of 2​𝒫⋅B​N​(K+1)2\mathcal{P}\cdot BN(K{+}1) FLOPs. The bytes transferred are b​𝒫b\mathcal{P} (loading the weights once), giving AItarget=2​𝒫⋅B​N​(K+1)/(b​𝒫)=2​B​N​(K+1)/b\text{AI}_{\text{target}}=2\mathcal{P}\cdot BN(K{+}1)/(b\mathcal{P})=2BN(K{+}1)/b. For FP16 (b=2b{=}2) this reduces to B​N​(K+1)BN(K{+}1). For comparison, autoregressive decoding achieves AI=2​B/b\text{AI}=2B/b and standard SD achieves AI=2​B​(K+1)/b\text{AI}=2B(K{+}1)/b when all KK draft tokens are accepted. When AItarget\text{AI}_{\text{target}} exceeds the hardware’s ridge point (peak FLOPs / peak bandwidth), the target pass becomes compute-bound and further increasing the effective batch size B​NBN no longer comes for free. ∎

Lemma D.2 (Full-cycle arithmetic intensity).

Over a full SMC-SD cycle (including KK draft forward passes), the arithmetic intensity is

AIcycle=2​B​N​(ρ​K+K+1)b⁡(ρ​K+1)≈2​B​N​(K+1)bwhen ​ρ≪1.\text{AI}_{\text{cycle}}=\frac{2BN(\rho K{+}K{+}1)}{b(\rho K+1)}\;\approx\;\frac{2BN(K{+}1)}{b}\quad\text{when }\rho\ll 1. (43)
Proof.

The total FLOPs over one cycle are 2​𝒫q⋅B​N​K+2​𝒫⋅B​N​(K+1)=2​𝒫​B​N​(ρ​K+K+1)2\mathcal{P}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}\cdot BNK+2\mathcal{P}\cdot BN(K{+}1)=2\mathcal{P}\,BN(\rho K+K+1): the draft model performs KK forward passes each processing B​NBN tokens, and the target model performs one pass processing B​N​(K+1)BN(K{+}1) tokens. The total bytes transferred are b​𝒫q⋅K+b​𝒫=b​𝒫​(ρ​K+1)b\mathcal{P}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}\cdot K+b\mathcal{P}=b\mathcal{P}(\rho K+1): the draft weights are loaded KK times and the target weights once. Dividing gives AIcycle=2​B​N​(ρ​K+K+1)/(b⁡(ρ​K+1))\text{AI}_{\text{cycle}}=2BN(\rho K+K+1)/(b(\rho K+1)). When ρ≪1\rho\ll 1, the draft-model terms become negligible and this simplifies to 2​B​N​(K+1)/b2BN(K{+}1)/b. ∎

D.2 Speedup Proofs

Lemma D.3 (Memory-bound speed-up).

If the target forward pass is memory bandwidth-bound (i.e. B​N​(K+1)≤RBN(K{+}1)\leq R, where RR is the hardware ridge-point batch size), the SMC-SD speed-up over autoregressive decoding is

S(mem)=K+1c​K+1,S^{(\text{mem})}=\frac{K+1}{cK+1}, (44)

independent of the effective batch size B​NBN.

Proof.

When the target forward pass is memory bandwidth-bound, loading the model weights dominates and the verification cost is approximately constant regardless of B​NBN. The cycle time is

tSMC-SD step(mem)=Tp​(c​K+1).t_{\text{SMC-SD step}}^{(\text{mem})}=T_{p}\bigl(cK+1\bigr). (45)

Since autoregressive decoding takes Tp​KT_{p}K seconds for KK tokens and each SMC-SD cycle produces K+1K{+}1 tokens per request, the speed-up is S(mem)=(K+1)/(c​K+1)S^{(\text{mem})}=(K{+}1)/(cK+1). Adding more particles or requests is “free” because the target weights are loaded only once regardless of B​NBN. ∎

Lemma D.4 (Compute-bound speed-up).

If the target forward pass is compute-bound (i.e. B​N​(K+1)>RBN(K{+}1)>R), the SMC-SD speed-up over autoregressive decoding is

S(comp)=K+1c^​(B​N)​K+B​N​(K+1)/R,S^{(\text{comp})}=\frac{K+1}{\hat{c}(BN)\,K+BN(K{+}1)/R}, (46)

where c^​(B​N)=max⁡(c,c⋅B​N/R)\hat{c}(BN)=\max(c,\,c\cdot BN/R) is the effective draft cost ratio and RR is the hardware ridge-point batch size in tokens.

Proof.

As B​N​(K+1)BN(K{+}1) grows, the arithmetic intensity of the target pass eventually exceeds the hardware ridge point, and the forward pass becomes compute-bound. In this regime, the target verification time scales linearly with the number of tokens processed. Let Tp(1)T_{p}^{(1)} denote the (memory-bound) time to decode a single token with the target model. The compute-bound verification of B​N​(K+1)BN(K{+}1) tokens takes approximately Tp(1)⋅B​N​(K+1)/RT_{p}^{(1)}\cdot BN(K{+}1)/R seconds, where R=peak FLOPs/peak bandwidth⋅b/2R=\text{peak FLOPs}\,/\,\text{peak bandwidth}\cdot b/2 tokens (with bb bytes per parameter). The draft model, which processes B​NBN tokens in parallel at each of its KK steps, may itself become compute-bound if B​N>RBN>R. In the compute-bound regime, the draft model’s per-step cost scales as c⋅B​N/Rc\cdot BN/R relative to Tp(1)T_{p}^{(1)}, since the draft model has c≈ρc\approx\rho times the cost of the target per token. Writing c^​(B​N)=max⁡(c,c⋅B​N/R)\hat{c}(BN)=\max(c,\,c\cdot BN/R) for the effective draft cost ratio, the cycle time becomes

tSMC-SD step(comp)=Tp(1)​(c^​(B​N)​K+B​N​(K+1)R).t_{\text{SMC-SD step}}^{(\text{comp})}=T_{p}^{(1)}\!\left(\hat{c}(BN)\,K+\frac{BN(K{+}1)}{R}\right). (47)

Since autoregressive decoding takes Tp(1)T_{p}^{(1)} per token, the speed-up is S(comp)=(K+1)/(c^​(B​N)​K+B​N​(K+1)/R)S^{(\text{comp})}=(K{+}1)/(\hat{c}(BN)K+BN(K{+}1)/R). ∎

Appendix E Speed-up Under Declining Acceptance Rate

Standard SD’s throughput is tightly coupled to the draft–target acceptance rate, which drops as sampling temperature increases (or more generally, as the draft and target distributions diverge). SMC-SD, by contrast, always outputs K+1K{+}1 tokens per round regardless of acceptance, so its throughput is largely temperature-invariant. Figure 6 plots the SMC-SD / SD throughput ratio across temperatures: the speed-up grows from ∼1.5×{\sim}1.5\times at T=0.2T{=}0.2 to ∼3×{\sim}3\times at T=1.0T{=}1.0. On average across temperatures, SMC-SD sequences incur only a ∼5%{\sim}5\% increase in negative log-likelihood under the target model compared to exact SD, confirming that the approximation quality remains high even as the throughput advantage widens.

Appendix F Power Sampling

One advantage of SMC is that it allows us to sample approximately from un-normalized target distributions whose normalizing constants are intractable. One such target distribution is the power distribution (Karan and Du, 2025), given by ppow​(𝒙)∝p​(𝒙)αp_{\textrm{pow}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}})\propto p({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}})^{\alpha} where 𝒙∈𝒳∗{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}\in{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}^{*}. In contrast to temperature sampling, which tempers the distribution of each token, power sampling tempers the distribution over entire strings. Applying SMC-SD to sample approximately from this distribution is simply a matter of weighting the draft model q{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}’s generated tokens by

wt(n)=p→​(xt(n)∣𝒙<t(n))αq→​(xt(n)∣𝒙<t(n)).{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}_{t}^{(n)}=\frac{{\overrightarrow{p}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{t}^{(n)}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}_{<t})^{\alpha}}{\overrightarrow{{\color[rgb]{0,0.88,0}q}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{t}^{(n)}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}_{<t})}. (48)

Prior work has proposed using SMC to sample approximately from the power distribution. PowerSMC (Azizi et al., 2026) proposes generating particles via temperature sampling

xt(n)∼p→(⋅∣𝒙(n)<t)α∑x∈𝒳p→​(x∣𝒙<t(n))α,{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}_{t}^{(n)}\sim\frac{{\overrightarrow{p}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}_{<t})^{\alpha}}{\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}}{\overrightarrow{p}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}_{<t})^{\alpha}}, (49)

weighting with importance weight equal to

wt(n)=∑x∈𝒳p→​(x∣𝒙<t(n))α,{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}w}_{t}^{(n)}=\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\mathcal{X}}}{\overrightarrow{p}}({\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}x}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.5508,0.0391,0.3477}\bm{x}}^{(n)}_{<t})^{\alpha}, (50)

and resampling after each batch of tokens is generated (if the ESS is less than a cutoff). The PowerSMC procedure can be expressed as a special case of the SMC-SD framework where K=1K=1, the bonus token is removed, and the target and draft models are the same. The authors prove that temperature sampling from the target model provides the locally variance-minimizing proposal for sampling from the power distribution. Figure 7 shows that sampling from the power distribution of an 8B Llama model with a 1B Llama draft model yields a 10% higher Pass@1 accuracy over the baseline target model. Accuracy for Pass@kk for k>1k>1 is greater than or equal to the baseline target model as well.

Llama 1B→\rightarrow8B

Question: Claire makes a 3 egg omelet every morning for breakfast. How many dozens of eggs will she eat in 4 weeks?

SMC-SD: Step 1: Convert 4 weeks to days — 4 weeks ×\times 7 days/week == 28 days. Step 2: Calculate the number of eggs in 28 days — 28 days ×\times 3 eggs/day == 84 eggs. Step 3: Convert the number of eggs from eggs to dozens — 84 eggs / 12 eggs/dozen == 7 dozens. The final answer is: 7.

Qwen 3B→\rightarrow14B

Question: A new program had 60 downloads in the first month. The number of downloads in the second month was three times as many as the downloads in the first month, but then reduced by 30% in the third month. How many downloads did the program have total over the three months?

SMC-SD: First month: 60 downloads. Second month: 3×60=1803\times 60=180 downloads. Third month: reduced by 30%, so 180×0.70=126180\times 0.70=126 downloads. Total: 60+180+126=36660+180+126=366.

Llama 1B→\rightarrow8B — Counting & Probability, Level 5

Problem: Pat is to select six cookies from a tray containing only chocolate chip, oatmeal, and peanut butter cookies. There are at least six of each of these three kinds of cookies on the tray. How many different assortments of six cookies can be selected?

SMC-SD: We can use combinations with repetition. Distributing 6 identical items into 3 distinct groups: C⁡(n+k−1,k)=C⁡(3+6−1,6)=C⁡(8,6)=8!/(6!×2!)=28C(n+k-1,k)=C(3+6-1,6)=C(8,6)=8!/(6!\times 2!)=28.

Qwen 3B→\rightarrow14B — Assess credibility

Instruction: How can you assess the credibility of a source of information, such as a news article or blog post, without relying solely on the reputation of the author or publisher?

SMC-SD: Assessing the credibility of a source of information, including a news article or blog post, is a matter of taking a few key steps to understand the reliability and quality of the information presented. Here”s a checklist of steps that can be followed to evaluate the credibility of the source:

  • •

    Check the Author and Publisher’s Background: Look for the author’s credentials, expertise, and the publication’s reputation. A reputable author or publisher is less likely to have a history of making false claims or spreading misinformation.

  • •

    Review the Bias and Methodology: Assess the sources of information used in the article or blog post. Check if the data or other sources are clearly stated and verified. Look for indications of bias—bias can come from multiple sources, leading to an incomplete or potentially misleading narrative.

  • •

    Check for Reproducibility of the Data: Determine whether the data used in the article or blog post can be reproduced. This is crucial to ensure that the information presented is verifiable. If the data could be easily modified, then the information is less credible.

  • •

    Evaluate the Relevance to the Topic: The article should be based on issues of relevance and current importance. The information should address a specific problem or discuss an issue of public interest. The author must also support their claims with facts and evidence.

  • •

    Check for Peer Reactions and Expert Consensus: The credibility of the source also depends on the extent to which other experts in the field agree with the information. Support from respected figures can significantly bolster the credibility of a source.

  • •

    Use External References and Other Sources: Look for credible references that support the claims made in the article or blog post. Cross-referencing can help verify the accuracy of the information presented.

  • •

    Look for a Balanced View: Ensure that the article or blog post provides a fair and balanced view of the topic. Avoid articles that are overly negative or sensationalistic.

  • •

    Check for Up to Date Information: Keep up with the latest developments in the field or topic being discussed. This can often provide the most reliable and up-to-date information.

By following these steps, you can effectively assess the credibility of a source of information, ensuring that you obtain accurate and trustworthy information.

Qwen 3B→\rightarrow14B — NumPy, Problem 292

Prompt: I want to figure out how to remove nan values from my array. For example, my array looks something like x = [1400, 1500, 1600, nan, nan, nan, 1700]. How can I remove the nan values from x to get something like [1400, 1500, 1600, 1700]?

SMC-SD:

import numpy as np

# Given array with nan values
x = np.array([1400, 1500, 1600, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, 1700])

# Filter out nan values
x_clean = x[~np.isnan(x)]

print(x_clean)
